description: I am a high school senior interested in aerospace engineering, physics, and programming. I have worked on projects involving rocket trajectory simulation, numerical modeling, and data analysis using Python. For Space Apps, I am interested in building a tool that uses NASA data to solve real engineering problems.
summary:
LunaWindow is an interactive lunar landing site analysis tool developed for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. It helps users compare potential landing locations and mission dates by analyzing solar illumination and direct to Earth geometric visibility using real astronomical data from NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) Horizons system.

Built with Python and Streamlit, LunaWindow allows users to select two lunar locations, specify observation periods, and visualize the positions of the Sun and Earth relative to an idealized lunar horizon. The application estimates simultaneous visibility windows, compares site conditions, and provides interactive sensitivity analysis to investigate how minimum elevation requirements affect potential mission operations.

Additional features include a schematic 3D Moon, a local horizon sky viewer, mission status indicators, and downloadable analysis results.

LunaWindow aims to make lunar mission planning constraints more accessible to students, educators, and space enthusiasts while demonstrating how location and timing influence potential solar power and communication opportunities.
details:
Overview

LunaWindow is a browser based lunar mission planning prototype designed to make it easier to compare potential landing locations and observation periods. It focuses on two important constraints for lunar surface missions: access to sunlight and geometric visibility of Earth for potential direct communication.

These considerations are particularly important near the Moon's south pole, where the Sun remains relatively low in the sky and small changes in location or timing can affect mission conditions.

How It Works

Users begin by entering the latitude and longitude of two lunar locations, selecting a starting date, and choosing an observation duration and sampling interval.

LunaWindow retrieves topocentric Sun and Earth ephemerides from NASA's JPL Horizons system through the Astroquery Python library. The application processes the returned timestamps, azimuths, and elevation angles to compare the two locations.

The software provides several interactive features:

  • Sun and Earth Elevation Analysis: Visualizes changes in elevation angle throughout the observation period.
  • Landing Site Comparison: Calculates the percentage of sampled observations when the Sun, Earth, or both are above an idealized lunar horizon.
  • Mission Operations Analyzer: Estimates simultaneous Sun/Earth visibility windows using linear interpolation between observation samples.
  • 3D Lunar Explorer: Displays a rotatable schematic Moon with markers representing the selected locations.
  • Local Horizon Sky Viewer: Displays the positions of the Sun and Earth using azimuth and elevation coordinates.
  • Mission Status Dashboard: Shows the geometric visibility conditions at a selected observation time.
  • Landing Window Robustness Analyzer: Allows users to adjust minimum Sun and Earth elevation requirements and observe their effects on estimated visibility.
  • Engineering Sensitivity Experiments: Automatically compares baseline, solar clearance, Earth clearance, and combined clearance scenarios.
  • Data Export: Allows users to download analysis results as CSV files.

Preliminary Findings

An initial analysis compared two test locations at 89° south latitude, separated by 30° in longitude, between November 15 and November 17, 2026.

Both sites had the Sun above the idealized horizon at every sampled observation. However, Site A had Earth above the horizon at approximately 5.9% of sampled observations, compared with 0% for Site B.

Using linear interpolation, LunaWindow estimated approximately 0.513 hours of simultaneous geometric visibility at Site A. Sensitivity testing demonstrated that the estimated window could disappear entirely when stricter elevation requirements were introduced.

These results illustrate how mission location and timing decisions can influence the availability of potentially useful illumination and communication conditions.

Technologies Used

LunaWindow was developed using Python, Streamlit, Astroquery, Astropy, NumPy, Pandas, and Plotly. GitHub is used for source code management, and the application is publicly hosted through Streamlit Community Cloud.

The application does not require specialized hardware or a high performance graphics computer.

Creativity and Intended Impact

LunaWindow combines astronomical data retrieval, numerical visibility window estimation, interactive visualization, and engineering sensitivity testing in a single accessible application.

Rather than only displaying astronomical positions, the tool helps users investigate how mission constraints affect the available operating periods at different lunar locations.

Its intended audience includes students, educators, space enthusiasts, and individuals interested in understanding lunar mission planning challenges.

Limitations and Future Development

LunaWindow is an exploratory engineering prototype, not a validated operational mission planning system.

The current analysis uses an idealized lunar horizon and does not account for obstruction by mountains or crater rims, eclipse conditions, solar panel orientation and efficiency, or communication link budgets. Visibility window estimates also depend on interpolation between discrete observation samples.

Future development could incorporate actual lunar topography, improved numerical validation, and more detailed power and communication models.
